facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: According to ancient Sanskrit literature, the Lord Krishna founded the holy city of Dwarka, which subsequently got submerged under sea.
facts.text: The Harivamsa describes Dvaravati as a coastal capital fortified with ramparts and moats that was reclaimed from the ocean by Krishna for the Yadavas.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The successive underwater investigations off Dwarka in about 4 to 12 m water depth have revealed the presence of a number of submerged stone building blocks such as remains of wall, pillar and bastion.
facts.text: Underwater explorations off the coast of Dwarka conducted by the National Institute of Oceanography between 1983 and 1992 revealed submerged stone masonry blocks, pillars, and bastions at depths reaching 12 metres.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: A group of 20 stone anchors from the waters of Dwarka, on the Gujarat Coast, India.
facts.text: Marine archaeologists from the National Institute of Oceanography documented a group of twenty stone anchors in the seabed waters off Dwarka.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: During field season of 2000-2001 four stone structures of circular in shape have been noticed in inter-tidal zone of Dwarka.
facts.text: During the 2000 to 2001 field season, National Institute of Oceanography researchers documented four circular stone structures located in the intertidal zone adjacent to the mouth of Gomati creek.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Earlier the Underwater Archaeology Wing had carried-out offshore and onshore excavations at Dwarka from 2005 to 2007. The coastal areas were examined during low tide where sculptures and stone anchors were discovered.
facts.text: The Underwater Archaeology Wing of the Archaeological Survey of India conducted onshore and offshore excavations at Dwarka between 2005 and 2007, discovering stone anchors and sculptures during low-tide examinations.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: A team of five archaeologists from the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), led by Prof. Alok Tripathi, Additional Director-General (Archaeology) has commenced groundbreaking underwater explorations off the coast of Dwarka.
facts.text: In February 2025, the Archaeological Survey of India deployed a five-member dive team to initiate updated underwater mapping and explorations near Gomati Creek.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The comparative study of surrounding sites indicates that the date of the structures of Dwarka may be between Historical period and late medieval period.
facts.text: Marine archaeologist S. R. Rao dated the submerged stone masonry and pottery to around 1500 BCE, whereas subsequent NIO researchers led by A. S. Gaur dated the stone anchors and structural remains to the historical and medieval eras.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Offshore explorations have brought to light a large number of stone structures, which appear to be the remains of an ancient jetty... natural factors like coastal erosion are primarily responsible for the destruction of the structures.
facts.text: While early excavation teams identified the submerged alignments as defensive walls of an epic-era city, later marine geologists and archaeologists argued that the blocks represent an ancient harbour jetty damaged by natural marine erosion.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Analysis of sea level versus ancient settlement suggests that around the Christian era sea level was lower by 2 m than the present.
facts.text: While alternative theories propose that a massive mid-Holocene flood submerged a 3,000-year-old city, NIO sea-level studies off Saurashtra indicate that the local sea level was approximately 2 metres lower during the early historical period.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Local folklore attributes the instant sinking of Krishna's golden citadel to a curse fulfilled thirty-six years after the great war.
facts.text: Popular regional folklore recounts that the golden city of Dwarka vanished under an overnight catastrophic tsunami thirty-six years after the Kurukshetra War due to an unalterable curse.
